summary:
North Gyeongsang Province stands under the national framework of South Korea, where consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal and criminalisation is concentrated in the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted, including the 2017 military operation that Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, in which 32 personnel were criminally charged and one soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm to a transgender person under this framework is the case of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Ministry of National Defence recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korea and the surgical condition attached to it has fallen away. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender people with minor children may have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required applicants to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions and does not permit same-sex couples to adopt jointly. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register, a right won through litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 that the government continued to appeal, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

No North Gyeongsang-specific trans ordinance, enforcement finding or incident series was located in the source inventory, so the province is scored against the national position. A visitor to North Gyeongsang should expect the same legal treatment documented elsewhere in South Korea.

Police advice telling a transitioning person to stay out of women's public restrooms has been held unlawful. The Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, in a case brought by a person transitioning from male to female who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020; the appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The same national framework produced a 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents, 41% of whom reported avoiding facilities out of fear.

Registered-sex change no longer requires surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning a gender change on surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Violence at Pride events is a national pattern rather than a provincial one: in Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, with organisers later filing charges against pastors and accusing police of inaction, while at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. Anti-LGBT mobilisation of this kind, and the policing response to it, is the adjacent risk a visitor should weigh when attending public events anywhere in South Korea.

Documented discrimination burdens are heavy and quantified. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

The one substantial advance for same-sex couples nationally is a landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights, which does not extend to marriage, civil unions or joint adoption.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.
localsOnly:
Trans teenagers in South Korea avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, includes the account of a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school who reported holding her bladder and leaving school early, and the researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Transgender people are barred from military service, which for residents of North Gyeongsang of conscript age means exclusion rather than the criminal exposure faced by serving personnel under article 92-6.

Residents seeking legal gender recognition now proceed without a surgical prerequisite, following the 8 May 2024 ruling that removed it and the 24 November 2022 Supreme Court decision permitting recognition for transgender parents of minor children who are unmarried.
outOfScopeNotes:
No North Gyeongsang-specific data on enforcement of article 92-6, on provincial or municipal anti-discrimination measures, or on documented incidents involving transgender residents was located in the source inventory. The province is therefore scored on national findings, and whether local practice diverges from the national record remains unresolved.

The source records the 8 May 2024 surgical-prerequisite ruling as the decision of a regional court in Yeongdong; the reporting does not set out the appellate history of that ruling, so its status as a final judgment is unresolved here.

Reports of police inaction at the Incheon Pride attack come from organisers' accusations; whether any officer was subsequently charged or disciplined is not sourced.

The parent framework notes that the Constitutional Court upheld Military Criminal Act article 92-6 in 2023; the inventory does not document prosecutions of that provision originating in North Gyeongsang, which remains unverified.
